title: Jaw Green
passages:
Kass didn't swing down. One boot on the pedal-rail's frame, the other on the frozen ballast, they breathed through their mouth and said it loud enough for the work light to carry: "J. Renner. That name's on Anza's overlap log. Teodoro countersigned it himself. So the two halves of this ticket on Brill's blank plate — they staple Culvert Nine to Nour's eleven short strikes in a document a desk can actually read."

The wind off the dead pumps didn't care. It tore the words and scattered them across the spur.

Miko didn't look down from the crew box. Her gloved fingers folded the half-torn J. Renner ticket slow and deliberate, like she was putting a letter back in an envelope, and slipped it into her coat's inner pocket. Then her other hand came out holding a second ticket — clean edges, fresh watermark, a name Kass didn't recognize and hadn't seen on any board, any log, any chalk tally in three nodes of riding the line.

"Never touched paper," Miko said. Her voice carried flat over the bearing whine settling in Kass's ears. "Never touched a desk. Never touched a seal."

She tore it clean across the watermark. The sound was small and final in the cold — paper fiber giving way, no ragged edge, no hesitation. Two perfect halves fluttered down into the work light's cone.

Saul didn't move their pencil. Their clipboard stayed pressed to their chest, the M. Varel sheet still open, the graphite tip hovering over a line they'd already written twice.

Brill didn't blink. She stood at the storeroom door with her hand knife at her belt and a child's bowl steady in her other hand, the steam rising from it the only warm thing in the yard. The child — maybe six, maybe seven, wrapped in three coats and a scarf that had seen better winters — watched the paper halves fall.

Kass let their breath out slow. Their knee ached where the bearing had bitten through the packing. "That one doesn't staple anything."

"No," Miko said. She climbed down the rig's ladder rung by rung, boots hitting the deck plate solid. "But it buys the unload. And the eleven cans go into the jaw. And the kid eats."

She landed light, rolled her shoulder, and walked toward the blank door plate without looking at Saul, without looking at Kass. The hand lamp still hung in the crew box window, burning steady against the dark.

Behind her, the blank rig's forward canister gave its fourth cold-cycle bite. The clamp ring sang against the collar, a sound like a bell struck wrong.
